consensus_summary: Jacob primarily represents Israel or the covenant people, with common secondary readings emphasizing the self-reliant supplanter transformed by grace.
book_summary: Jacob denotes the crooked, supplanting covenant person or people specifically in the condition preceding the transformed identity called Israel.
consensus_core_identification: Jacob is the patriarchal and corporate embodiment of Israel, God's covenant people.
book_core_identification: Jacob is the covenant person or people in a crooked, supplanting, pre-transformation condition, distinguished from the transformed name Israel.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus broadly allows “Jacob” and “Israel” to designate the same covenant people interchangeably, including after the patriarch's renaming. The book restricts “Jacob” to their deceitful or untransformed condition and reserves “Israel” for the transformed identity.
material_contradiction: There is no replacement of the covenant-person/people referent. The disagreement concerns whether Jacob is a general name for Israel or a conditionally distinct, pre-transformation designation.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus category of the covenant patriarch and people but imposes a sharper Jacob-versus-Israel distinction. This distinction is already recognizable among the consensus alternatives, especially the allegory of Jacob as the natural or fleshly state and Israel as the transformed state, so it is not novel. It nevertheless materially narrows and reclassifies the broader consensus usage.
strongest_objection: Genesis 27:36 directly supports the characterization “supplanting,” and Jeremiah 17:9 supports human crookedness generally. Neither citation alone establishes that every symbolic use of Jacob denotes a pre-transformation covenant condition; moreover, prophetic texts often use “Jacob” and “Israel” in parallel for the same people even after the renaming.
